claim: Climatic warming can shift community composition driven by the colonization-extinction dynamics of species with different thermal preferences.
source: Climatic warming can shift community composition driven by the colonization-extinction dynamics of species with different thermal preferences; but simultaneously, habitat fragmentation can mediate species' responses to warming.
evidence: This is a general statement about climate warming effects that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Habitat fragmentation can mediate species' responses to warming.
source: Climatic warming can shift community composition driven by the colonization-extinction dynamics of species with different thermal preferences; but simultaneously, habitat fragmentation can mediate species' responses to warming.
evidence: This is a general statement about habitat fragmentation effects that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Bird data was collected over 10 years of climate warming in a reservoir subtropical island system.
source: As this potential interactive effect has proven difficult to test empirically, we collected data on birds over 10 years of climate warming in a reservoir subtropical island system that was formed 65 years ago.
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology used in the study.

claim: The reservoir subtropical island system was formed 65 years ago.
source: As this potential interactive effect has proven difficult to test empirically, we collected data on birds over 10 years of climate warming in a reservoir subtropical island system that was formed 65 years ago.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system's history.

claim: Thermophilization was driven by increasing warm-adapted species and decreasing cold-adapted species in terms of trends in colonization rate, extinction rate, occupancy rate and population size.
source: We found thermophilization driven by increasing warm-adapted species and decreasing cold-adapted species in terms of trends in colonization rate, extinction rate, occupancy rate and population size.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Colonization rates of warm-adapted species increased faster temporally on smaller or less isolated islands.
source: Critically, colonization rates of warm-adapted species increased faster temporally on smaller or less isolated islands; cold-adapted species generally were lost more quickly temporally on closer islands.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Cold-adapted species generally were lost more quickly temporally on closer islands.
source: Critically, colonization rates of warm-adapted species increased faster temporally on smaller or less isolated islands; cold-adapted species generally were lost more quickly temporally on closer islands.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Dispersal limitation and microclimate buffering are primary proxies by which habitat fragmentation mediates species range shift.
source: This provides support for dispersal limitation and microclimate buffering as primary proxies by which habitat fragmentation mediates species range shift.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on the observed patterns.

claim: Climate warming leads to shifts in species' distributions toward cooler regions.
source: One widespread consequence of anthropogenic-caused climate warming is the shift in species' distributions toward cooler regions (Chen et al., 2011; La Sorte and Thompson, 2007; Thomas and Lennon, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: As species move across the globe, the composition of community changes, with species both colonizing and departing.
source: As species move across the globe, the composition of community changes, with species both colonizing and departing (Menéndez et al., 2006; Tingley and Beissinger, 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Colonizing and departing species will be drawn depending on their traits, such as being warm-adapted versus cold-adapted.
source: yet colonizing and departing species are unlikely to be randomly drawn from species pools, but instead will be drawn depending on their traits, such as being warm-adapted versus cold-adapted.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on ecological theory about species traits and climate responses.

claim: A warming climate should lead to compositional shifts toward relatively more warm-adapted species in local communities.
source: As a result, a warming climate should lead to compositional shifts toward relatively more warm-adapted species in local communities (Thomas et al., 2006), a phenomenon termed 'thermophilization' (Feeley et al., 2020; Gottfried et al., 2012; Zellweger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thermophilization is the phenomenon of compositional shifts toward relatively more warm-adapted species in local communities.
source: As a result, a warming climate should lead to compositional shifts toward relatively more warm-adapted species in local communities (Thomas et al., 2006), a phenomenon termed 'thermophilization' (Feeley et al., 2020; Gottfried et al., 2012; Zellweger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thermophilization can be measured by a temporal increase in the Community Temperature Index (CTI).
source: In practice, thermophilization can be measured by a temporal increase in the Community Temperature Index (CTI; Devictor et al., 2008) – an estimation of the average temperature experienced by all species in an assemblage throughout their respective ranges.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CTI is an estimation of the average temperature experienced by all species in an assemblage throughout their respective ranges.
source: In practice, thermophilization can be measured by a temporal increase in the Community Temperature Index (CTI; Devictor et al., 2008) – an estimation of the average temperature experienced by all species in an assemblage throughout their respective ranges.
evidence: This is a definition of CTI supported by a citation.

claim: Thermophilization of communities is usually accompanied by an increase in warm-adapted species and a decrease in cold-adapted species.
source: While thermophilization of communities is usually accompanied by an increase in warm-adapted species and a decrease in cold-adapted species (Curley et al., 2022; Princé and Zuckerberg, 2015; Tayleur et al., 2016; Figure 1a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Thermophilization is spatially heterogeneous and depends on the availability of current habitat and the ability to disperse into newly suitable habitats.
source: this process is usually spatially heterogeneous and depends on the availability of current habitat and the ability to disperse into newly suitable habitats (Gaüzère et al., 2017; Richard et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Habitat fragmentation is defined as the process of transforming continuous habitat into spatially isolated and small patches.
source: Habitat fragmentation, usually defined as the process of transforming continuous habitat into spatially isolated and small patches (Fahrig, 2003)
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: Habitat fragmentation has been hypothesized to have interactive effects with climate change on community dynamics.
source: Habitat fragmentation, usually defined as the process of transforming continuous habitat into spatially isolated and small patches (Fahrig, 2003), in particular, has been hypothesized to have interactive effects with climate change on community dynamics.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on ecological theory and previous research.

claim: Patch area and isolation are two of the most used measures of habitat fragmentation.
source: Among the various ways in which habitat fragmentation is conceptualized and measured, patch area and isolation are two of the most used measures (Fahrig, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Habitat fragmentation usually alters both habitat spatial structure and microclimate characteristics.
source: Specifically, habitat fragmentation usually alters both habitat spatial structure and microclimate characteristics (Ewers and Banks-Leite, 2013; Fahrig, 2003)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Habitat spatial structure and microclimate characteristics can influence thermophilization processes.
source: Specifically, habitat fragmentation usually alters both habitat spatial structure and microclimate characteristics (Ewers and Banks-Leite, 2013; Fahrig, 2003), either of which can influence thermophilization processes (Gaüzère et al., 2017; Platts et al., 2019; Richard et al., 2021; Zellweger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fragmented habitats may more weakly buffer macroclimate than intact habitats.
source: First, fragmented habitats may more weakly buffer macroclimate than intact habitats (Ewers and Banks-Leite, 2013), resulting in fragmented patches experiencing relatively higher temperatures.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fragmented patches experience relatively higher temperatures due to weaker buffering of macroclimate.
source: First, fragmented habitats may more weakly buffer macroclimate than intact habitats (Ewers and Banks-Leite, 2013), resulting in fragmented patches experiencing relatively higher temperatures.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the cited research about microclimate buffering.

claim: Increased temperature in small patches may boost the colonization or population growth rate of warm-adapted species.
source: Increased temperature, especially in small patches, may boost the colonization or population growth rate of warm-adapted species but cause higher extinction risk or demographic declines of cold-adapted species (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis illustrated in Figure 1b based on ecological theory.

claim: Increased temperature in small patches may cause higher extinction risk or demographic declines of cold-adapted species.
source: Increased temperature, especially in small patches, may boost the colonization or population growth rate of warm-adapted species but cause higher extinction risk or demographic declines of cold-adapted species (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis illustrated in Figure 1b based on ecological theory.

claim: The microclimate mechanism has been proposed as an important factor driving thermophilization in plant communities.
source: This microclimate mechanism has been proposed as an important factor driving thermophilization in plant communities (Zellweger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Larger patches generally contain higher habitat heterogeneity and therefore also encompass higher food availability and microrefugia.
source: Second, larger patches generally contain higher habitat heterogeneity and therefore also encompass higher food availability and microrefugia (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A diversity of habitats and resources is closely related to a species' successful establishment and can act as a buffer against extinction under climate change.
source: A diversity of habitats and resources is closely related to a species' successful establishment and can act as a buffer against extinction under climate change (Luoto and Heikkinen, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Higher habitat diversity can boost the ability of niche tracking in bird communities.
source: For instance, higher habitat diversity can boost the ability of niche tracking in bird communities (Gaüzère et al., 2017), mainly by fostering species' dispersal into new, climatically suitable sites.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In areas where topography generates greater microclimate variation, population losses of plants and insects due to climate change are substantially reduced.
source: Similarly, in areas where topography generates greater microclimate variation, population losses of plants and insects due to climate change are substantially reduced (Suggitt et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The reduction in habitat heterogeneity associated with higher fragmentation will intensify the loss of cold-adapted species and weaken the colonization of warm-adapted species.
source: We thus expect that the reduction in habitat heterogeneity associated with higher fragmentation will intensify the loss of cold-adapted species and weaken the colonization of warm-adapted species (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a hypothesis illustrated in Figure 1c based on ecological theory.

claim: Habitat fragmentation could prevent or interrupt species' dispersal which is essential for them to track suitable climatic niches.
source: Third, habitat fragmentation could prevent or interrupt species' dispersal which is essential for them to track suitable climatic niches (McGuire et al., 2016; Opdam and Wascher, 2004; Thomas et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dispersal limitation comes from higher mortality rate with increasing dispersal distance during searching for suitable patches.
source: This limitation may come from higher mortality rate with increasing dispersal distance during searching for suitable patches (Brooker et al., 1999), and will influence the colonization-extinction dynamics underlying climate response (Fourcade et al., 2021; Hylander and Ehrlén, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Habitat fragmentation renders habitats to be too isolated to be colonized, causing sedentary butterflies to lag more behind climate warming in Britain than mobile ones.
source: For example, habitat fragmentation renders habitats to be too isolated to be colonized, causing sedentary butterflies to lag more behind climate warming in Britain than mobile ones (Warren et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Less isolated patches should experience increasing rate in colonization of warm-adapted species under warming.
source: All things being equal, less isolated patches should experience increasing rate in colonization of warm-adapted species under warming, benefitting from near sources of species; meanwhile, cold-adapted species should experience higher extinction rates on less isolated patches because they can emigrate easily from these patches under climate warming (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a hypothesis illustrated in Figure 1d based on ecological theory.

claim: Cold-adapted species should experience higher extinction rates on less isolated patches because they can emigrate easily from these patches under climate warming.
source: All things being equal, less isolated patches should experience increasing rate in colonization of warm-adapted species under warming, benefitting from near sources of species; meanwhile, cold-adapted species should experience higher extinction rates on less isolated patches because they can emigrate easily from these patches under climate warming (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a hypothesis illustrated in Figure 1d based on ecological theory.

claim: Few empirical studies have considered multiple mechanisms of habitat fragmentation effects on climate-induced community dynamics simultaneously.
source: Although the overall effect of habitat fragmentation on climate-induced community dynamics has been established, few empirical studies have ever considered these multiple mechanisms simultaneously.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The Thousand Island Lake reservoir island system was formed 65 years ago due to dam construction.
source: Here, we use 10 years of bird community data in a subtropical land-bridge island system (Thousand Island Lake, TIL, China, Figure 2) during a period of consistent climatic warming (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) to explore whether and how community thermal niche composition responds to climate change and how habitat fragmentation mediates the process. This reservoir island system was formed 65 years ago due to dam construction.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system's history.

claim: The study period experienced consistent climatic warming.
source: Here, we use 10 years of bird community data in a subtropical land-bridge island system (Thousand Island Lake, TIL, China, Figure 2) during a period of consistent climatic warming (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 which shows temperature data.

claim: The number of species detected in surveys on each island across the study period averaged 13.37±6.26 species.
source: The number of species detected in surveys on each island across the study period averaged 13.37±6.26 (mean ± SD) species, ranging from 2 to 40 species, with an observed gamma diversity of 60 species.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data.

claim: The number of species detected ranged from 2 to 40 species.
source: The number of species detected in surveys on each island across the study period averaged 13.37±6.26 (mean ± SD) species, ranging from 2 to 40 species, with an observed gamma diversity of 60 species.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data.

claim: The observed gamma diversity was 60 species.
source: The number of species detected in surveys on each island across the study period averaged 13.37±6.26 (mean ± SD) species, ranging from 2 to 40 species, with an observed gamma diversity of 60 species.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data.

claim: The STI of all 60 birds averaged 19.94±3.58°C.
source: The STI of all 60 birds averaged 19.94±3.58°C (mean ± SD) and ranged from 9.30°C (Cuculus canorus) to 27.20°C (Prinia inornate), with a median of 20.63°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data shown in figures.

claim: STI ranged from 9.30°C (Cuculus canorus) to 27.20°C (Prinia inornate).
source: The STI of all 60 birds averaged 19.94±3.58°C (mean ± SD) and ranged from 9.30°C (Cuculus canorus) to 27.20°C (Prinia inornate), with a median of 20.63°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data shown in figures.

claim: The median STI was 20.63°C.
source: The STI of all 60 birds averaged 19.94±3.58°C (mean ± SD) and ranged from 9.30°C (Cuculus canorus) to 27.20°C (Prinia inornate), with a median of 20.63°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data shown in figures.

claim: STI of resident species (n=47) and summer visitors (n=13) did not show a significant difference.
source: STI of resident species (n=47) and summer visitors (n=13) did not show a significant difference (t-test: t=0.23, df = 17.82, p=0.82).
evidence: This is a result from a statistical test performed on the study's data.

claim: No significant correlation was found between STI and species' ecological traits including dispersal ability, body size, body mass and clutch size.
source: No significant correlation was found between STI and species' ecological traits; specifically, the continuous variables of dispersal ability, body size, body mass and clutch size (Pearson correlations for each, |r|<0.22)
evidence: This is a result from statistical tests performed on the study's data.

claim: No significant correlation was found between STI and the categorial variables of diet, active layer, and residence type.
source: No significant correlation was found between STI and species' ecological traits; specifically, the continuous variables of dispersal ability, body size, body mass and clutch size (Pearson correlations for each, |r|<0.22), and the categorial variables of diet (carnivorous/omnivorous/herbivory), active layer (canopy/mid/low), and residence type (resident species/summer visitor).
evidence: This is a result from statistical tests performed on the study's data.

claim: At the landscape scale, occurrence-based CTI showed no trend.
source: At the landscape scale, considering species detected across the study area, occurrence-based CTI (CTIoccur; see section STI and CTI) showed no trend (posterior mean temporal trend = 0.414; 95% CrI: –12.751, 13.554)
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: At the landscape scale, abundance-based CTI showed a significant increasing trend.
source: At the landscape scale, considering species detected across the study area, occurrence-based CTI (CTIoccur; see section STI and CTI) showed no trend (posterior mean temporal trend = 0.414; 95% CrI: –12.751, 13.554) but abundance-based CTI (CTIabun; see section STI and CTI) showed a significant increasing trend (temporal trend [mean ± SE]=0.327 ± 0.041, t=7.989, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: Significant increases in CTI were found for both occurrence- and abundance-based indices at the individual transect level.
source: When measuring CTI trends for individual transects (expressed as °C/unit year), we found significant increases in CTI for both occurrence- (mean temporal trend = 0.124; 95% CrI: 0.108, 0.137) and abundance-based indices (temporal trend = 0.320 ± 0.021, t493=15.534, p<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was a weak positive linear relationship between STI and species-specific temporal occupancy trends.
source: Comparing across species with different thermal affinities, we found a weak positive linear relationship between STI and species-specific temporal occupancy trends (t-test: slope = 0.206, t58=1.766, p=0.082; Figure 4a)
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Warm-adapted species were marginally more likely to increase in occurrence over time.
source: Comparing across species with different thermal affinities, we found a weak positive linear relationship between STI and species-specific temporal occupancy trends (t-test: slope = 0.206, t58=1.766, p=0.082; Figure 4a), indicating warm-adapted species were marginally more likely to increase in occurrence over time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical result from the study's data.

claim: There was a significant positive relationship between STI and species' temporal trends in colonization.
source: Decomposing occurrence change to dynamic parameters; however, we found a significant positive relationship between STI and species' temporal trends in colonization (t-test: slope = 0.259, p=0.043) and a significant negative relationship between STI and species' temporal trends in extinction (t-test: slope = –0.414, p=0.015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significant negative relationship between STI and species' temporal trends in extinction.
source: Decomposing occurrence change to dynamic parameters; however, we found a significant positive relationship between STI and species' temporal trends in colonization (t-test: slope = 0.259, p=0.043) and a significant negative relationship between STI and species' temporal trends in extinction (t-test: slope = –0.414, p=0.015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Warm-adapted species generally increased in occupancy over time, driven by an increase in colonization probability and a decrease in extinction probability.
source: Thus, warm-adapted species generally increased in occupancy over time, which was driven by an increase in colonization probability and a decrease in extinction probability; in contrast, cold-adapted species generally decreased in occupancy over time, which was driven by an increase in extinction probability and a decrease in colonization probability (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results from the study's data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Cold-adapted species generally decreased in occupancy over time, driven by an increase in extinction probability and a decrease in colonization probability.
source: Thus, warm-adapted species generally increased in occupancy over time, which was driven by an increase in colonization probability and a decrease in extinction probability; in contrast, cold-adapted species generally decreased in occupancy over time, which was driven by an increase in extinction probability and a decrease in colonization probability (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results from the study's data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There was a strong correlation (r=-0.77) between species' trends in colonization and extinction probabilities.
source: Considering all species, the influence of a thermal-association gradient underlying occurrence dynamics resulted in a particularly strong correlation between species' trends in colonization and extinction probabilities (Pearson correlation r=–0.77; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There was a strong positive relationship between STI and each species' temporal trend in abundance.
source: Similar patterns were found for abundance, where we detected a strong positive relationship (t-test: slope = 0.153, t58=3.047, p=0.003) between STI and each species' temporal trend in abundance: warm-adapted species generally increased abundance while cold-adapted species decreased over 10 years (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Warm-adapted species generally increased abundance while cold-adapted species decreased over 10 years.
source: Similar patterns were found for abundance, where we detected a strong positive relationship (t-test: slope = 0.153, t58=3.047, p=0.003) between STI and each species' temporal trend in abundance: warm-adapted species generally increased abundance while cold-adapted species decreased over 10 years (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results from the study's data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: At the island scale, both total abundance and total species richness increased significantly for the warm-adapted species group.
source: At the island scale, both total abundance and total species richness increased significantly for the warm-adapted species group while both responses significantly decreased for the cold-adapted species (richness trend, P<0.001; total abundance trend, p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the island scale, both total abundance and total species richness significantly decreased for the cold-adapted species.
source: At the island scale, both total abundance and total species richness increased significantly for the warm-adapted species group while both responses significantly decreased for the cold-adapted species (richness trend, P<0.001; total abundance trend, p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both colonization and extinction probabilities showed evidence of being moderated by fragmentation.
source: Both colonization and extinction probabilities showed evidence of being moderated by fragmentation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 5.

claim: On islands nearer to the mainland, warm-adapted species (15 out of 15 investigated species) increased their colonization probability at a higher rate over time.
source: In particular, the effect of isolation on temporal dynamics of thermophilization was relatively consistent across cold- (Figure 5a) and warm-adapted species (Figure 5b); specifically, on islands nearer to the mainland, warm-adapted species (15 out of 15 investigated species) increased their colonization probability at a higher rate over time, while most cold-adapted species (21 out of 23 species) increased their extinction probability at a higher rate.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 5.

claim: On islands nearer to the mainland, most cold-adapted species (21 out of 23 species) increased their extinction probability at a higher rate.
source: In particular, the effect of isolation on temporal dynamics of thermophilization was relatively consistent across cold- (Figure 5a) and warm-adapted species (Figure 5b); specifically, on islands nearer to the mainland, warm-adapted species (15 out of 15 investigated species) increased their colonization probability at a higher rate over time, while most cold-adapted species (21 out of 23 species) increased their extinction probability at a higher rate.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For most warm-adapted species (11 out of 15 investigated species), colonization rates increased faster over time on smaller islands.
source: Island area, in contrast, had a more mixed role in moderating colonization/extinction rates across species. For most warm-adapted species (11 out of 15 investigated species; Figure 5b), colonization rates increased faster over time on smaller islands (i.e., negative area:year interaction term)
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The colonization rates of four warm-adapted species increased faster on larger islands, including Dendrocitta formosae which showed the only significant positive interactive effect.
source: however, the colonization rates of the other four species increased faster on larger islands, including the only significant positive interactive effect (Dendrocitta formosae).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: For cold-adapted species, extinction rates were approximately equally split between increasing faster on smaller islands (12 out of 23 species) and increasing faster on larger islands (11 out of 23 species).
source: For cold-adapted species, extinction rates were approximately equally split between increasing faster on smaller islands (12 out of 23 species) and increasing faster on larger islands (11 out of 23 species), including two species, Spizixos semitorques and Pericrocotus cantonensis, which showed significantly increasing rates of extinction on larger islands.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: Spizixos semitorques and Pericrocotus cantonensis showed significantly increasing rates of extinction on larger islands.
source: For cold-adapted species, extinction rates were approximately equally split between increasing faster on smaller islands (12 out of 23 species) and increasing faster on larger islands (11 out of 23 species), including two species, Spizixos semitorques and Pericrocotus cantonensis, which showed significantly increasing rates of extinction on larger islands.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: Community thermal niche composition was changing directionally, mainly through gains in warm-adapted species and individuals and losses in cold-adapted species and individuals.
source: Our results confirm that community thermal niche composition was changing directionally, mainly through gains in warm-adapted species and individuals and losses in cold-adapted species and individuals.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: Colonization rates of most warm-adapted species tended to increase faster on smaller and less isolated islands.
source: We further found that habitat fragmentation influences two processes of thermophilization: colonization rates of most warm-adapted species tended to increase faster on smaller and less isolated islands, while the loss rates of most cold-adapted species tended to be exacerbated on less isolated islands.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: The loss rates of most cold-adapted species tended to be exacerbated on less isolated islands.
source: We further found that habitat fragmentation influences two processes of thermophilization: colonization rates of most warm-adapted species tended to increase faster on smaller and less isolated islands, while the loss rates of most cold-adapted species tended to be exacerbated on less isolated islands.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: Thermophilization has been found in many taxa.
source: Although thermophilization has been found in many taxa (Lajeunesse and Fourcade, 2023) and is more apparent in the tropics than in temperate zones (Freeman et al., 2021), there are few empirical demonstrations of this process in subtropical fragmented systems.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thermophilization is more apparent in the tropics than in temperate zones.
source: Although thermophilization has been found in many taxa (Lajeunesse and Fourcade, 2023) and is more apparent in the tropics than in temperate zones (Freeman et al., 2021), there are few empirical demonstrations of this process in subtropical fragmented systems.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There are few empirical demonstrations of thermophilization in subtropical fragmented systems.
source: Although thermophilization has been found in many taxa (Lajeunesse and Fourcade, 2023) and is more apparent in the tropics than in temperate zones (Freeman et al., 2021), there are few empirical demonstrations of this process in subtropical fragmented systems.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Decadal-scale thermophilization was evident in both occurrence- and abundance-based metrics.
source: We found decadal-scale thermophilization evident in both occurrence- and abundance-based metrics, although the response was considerably stronger for abundance.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The thermophilization response was considerably stronger for abundance than occurrence.
source: We found decadal-scale thermophilization evident in both occurrence- and abundance-based metrics, although the response was considerably stronger for abundance.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Abundance-weighted CTI generally responds more quickly than occurrence-based CTI given climatic warming.
source: This result is consistent with work in other systems, where abundance-weighted CTI generally responds more quickly than occurrence-based CTI given climatic warming (Devictor et al., 2008; Lindström et al., 2013; Oliver et al., 2017; Tayleur et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thermophilization of bird communities was mostly due to occurrence dynamics within the region, rather than exogenous community turnover outside the region.
source: Notably, when tested on the landscape scale (versus on individual island communities), only the abundance-based thermophilization trend was significant, indicating thermophilization of bird communities was mostly due to occurrence dynamics within the region, rather than exogenous community turnover outside the region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on the difference between landscape and island-level results.

claim: The pattern of increasing occupancy and abundance of warm-adapted species and decreasing occupancy and abundance of cold-adapted species is consistent with many previous studies conducted in continuous habitats in Europe or North America.
source: Consistent with our expectation, we found an overall increase in occupancy and abundance of warm-adapted species and a decrease in occupancy and abundance of cold-adapted species, which together contributed to thermophilization. This pattern is consistent with many previous studies conducted in continuous habitats in Europe or North America both for breeding and non-breeding bird communities (Curley et al., 2022; Princé and Zuckerberg, 2015; Tayleur et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: STI is an effective broad indicator of relative climatic vulnerability within a community.
source: Following that STI is predictably related to temporal trends in colonization and extinction rate (Figure 4), we can conclude that STI is an effective broad indicator of relative climatic vulnerability within a community, where species with relatively higher thermal preferences are generally poised to benefit from local climate warming and vice versa.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on the observed relationships.

claim: Species with relatively higher thermal preferences are generally poised to benefit from local climate warming.
source: Following that STI is predictably related to temporal trends in colonization and extinction rate (Figure 4), we can conclude that STI is an effective broad indicator of relative climatic vulnerability within a community, where species with relatively higher thermal preferences are generally poised to benefit from local climate warming and vice versa.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on the observed relationships.

claim: Relationships have been established between STI and species' population trend.
source: This conclusion is supported by studies that have established relationships between STI and species' population trend (Pearce-Higgins et al., 2015; Rigal et al., 2023), species' contribution analysis (Tayleur et al., 2016), or spatial occupancy (Anderson et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Temperature is related to species' survival through food resources, foraging time, and thermoregulatory requirements.
source: There are numerous reasons why we would expect temperature to strongly drive community change, as temperature is related to species' survival through food resources, foraging time, and thermoregulatory requirements (Dunn and Møller, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Thermophilization of avian communities in North America is mainly owed to the species that have increased in both range and population size.
source: For example, thermophilization of avian communities in North America is mainly owed to the species that have increased in both range and population size (Curley et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Contemporary latitudinal range shifts are thought to be primarily resultant of the expansion of polar margins of equatorial-distributed species.
source: Contemporary latitudinal range shifts are thought to be primarily resultant of the expansion of polar margins of equatorial-distributed species (La Sorte and Thompson, 2007; Thomas and Lennon, 1999), possibly due to extinction lags at equatorial margins (La Sorte and Jetz, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TIL is near the cold edge of most warm-adapted species like Hemixos castanonotus, Pericrocotus solaris, and Lonchura punctulate.
source: TIL is near the cold edge of most warm-adapted species like Hemixos castanonotus, Pericrocotus solaris, and Lonchura punctulate.
evidence: This is a statement about the geographic position of the study site relative to species distributions.

claim: Most birds in China should move upslope or poleward under climate change.
source: Combined with the prediction that most birds in China should move upslope or poleward under climate change (Hu et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Local climate will continue to shift warm-adapted species toward a thermal optimum, predicting continued population growth in the near future for these species.
source: we infer that local climate will continue to shift these warm-adapted species toward a thermal optimum, predicting continued population growth in the near future for these species (Sagarin and Gaines, 2002).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the study's findings and cited research.

claim: Extinctions are more difficult to detect than range expansions, partly due to temporal lags.
source: Meanwhile, most cold-adapted species in our system demonstrated increasing extinction rates over time. Extinctions are more difficult to detect than range expansions, partly due to temporal lags (Thomas et al., 2006; Thomas and Lennon, 1999) but also due to pervasive bias of false absences in time series data (Tingley and Beissinger, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Species' extinctions are more likely to be mediated by factors such as rainfall, species interactions, and changes in vegetation.
source: Moreover, species' extinctions are more likely to be mediated by factors such as rainfall, species interactions, and changes in vegetation (Paquette and Hargreaves, 2021; Thomas and Lennon, 1999), which will further lead to unequal rates of extinction relative to colonization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Not all warm-adapted species increased (in abundance or occupancy) and not all cold-adapted species decreased.
source: Despite the general trend, not all warm-adapted species increased (in abundance or occupancy) and not all cold-adapted species decreased.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's data analysis.

claim: Not all species contributed equally to the process of thermophilization.
source: In other words, not all species contributed equally to the process of thermophilization, as has been seen elsewhere (Tayleur et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research and the study's observations.

claim: Isolation from population sources can limit the dispersal that underlies range shifts.
source: As expected, the mediating effect of isolation on the two main processes of thermophilization was relatively consistent, with warm-adapted species colonizing faster and cold-adapted species being extirpated faster on islands nearer to the mainland. This indicates that isolation from population sources can limit the dispersal that underlies range shifts, supporting the general perception that habitat fragmentation is thought to impede climate-driven range expansions (Opdam and Wascher, 2004) or even block them (Warren et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Temperature buffering ability was diminished on smaller islands.
source: To investigate this mechanistic hypothesis more thoroughly, using understory air temperature data monitored on 20 islands in the breeding season in 2022, we found that temperature buffering ability indeed was diminished on smaller islands (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), further supporting microclimate as a primary driver of fragmentation's mediation of thermophilization (Zellweger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a result from additional temperature data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microclimate is a primary driver of fragmentation's mediation of thermophilization.
source: To investigate this mechanistic hypothesis more thoroughly, using understory air temperature data monitored on 20 islands in the breeding season in 2022, we found that temperature buffering ability indeed was diminished on smaller islands (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), further supporting microclimate as a primary driver of fragmentation's mediation of thermophilization (Zellweger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Areas with greater amounts of habitat featured lower extinction rates of cold-adapted butterfly species.
source: The increased extinction rate of some cold-adapted species on smaller islands is also consistent with the hypothesized impacts of reduced habitat heterogeneity (Figure 1c). Previous studies found that areas with greater amounts of habitat featured lower extinction rates of cold-adapted butterfly species (Fourcade et al., 2021), possibly by facilitating movement to colder microclimates (Suggitt et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Habitat diversity increased significantly with island area instead of isolation in the TIL system.
source: Habitat diversity, including the observed number of species, the rarefied species richness per island, species density and the rarefied species richness per unit area, all increased significantly with island area instead of isolation in our system (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research in the same system.

claim: Predators like snakes and felids may increase activity under climate warming.
source: Although post hoc, we speculate that these species face stronger predation pressures on larger islands. For example, predators like snakes and felids may also increase activity under climate warming (DeGregorio et al., 2015), but these predators only exist in our system on the larger islands.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Better connected landscapes should be developed to remove dispersal constraints and facilitate species' relocation to the best suitable microclimate.
source: Overall, our findings have important implications for conservation practices. Firstly, we confirmed the role of isolation in limiting range shifting. Better connected landscapes should be developed to remove dispersal constraints and facilitate species' relocation to the best suitable microclimate.
evidence: This is a conservation recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Small patches can foster the establishment of newly adapted warm-adapted species while large patches can act as refugia for cold-adapted species.
source: Second, small patches can foster the establishment of newly adapted warm-adapted species while large patches can act as refugia for cold-adapted species.
evidence: This is a conservation recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Preserving patches of diverse sizes can act as stepping stones or shelters in a warming climate depending on the thermal affinity of species.
source: Therefore, preserving patches of diverse sizes can act as stepping stones or shelters in a warming climate depending on the thermal affinity of species.
evidence: This is a conservation recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: The Thousand Island Lake was formed in 1959 following the construction of the Xin'anjiang Dam for hydroelectricity.
source: The Thousand Island Lake (TIL), located in eastern China, was formed in 1959 following the construction of the Xin'anjiang Dam for hydroelectricity (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system's history.

claim: When the lake is at its highest, there are 1078 islands with an area larger than 0.25 ha.
source: When the lake is at its highest, there are 1078 islands with an area larger than 0.25 ha.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system.

claim: About 90% of the forested areas are dominated by Masson pine (Pinus massoniana) in the canopy and broad‐leaved species in the sub‐canopy and understory.
source: Currently, about 90% of the forested areas are dominated by Masson pine (Pinus massoniana) in the canopy and broad‐leaved species (e.g. Loropetalum chinensei, Vaccinium carlesii, and Rhododendron simsii) in the sub‐canopy and understory (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system supported by a citation.

claim: The climatic zone is a typical monsoon climate.
source: The climatic zone is a typical monsoon climate.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system's climate.

claim: The precipitation is mainly concentrated between April and June with an average yearly rainfall of 1430 mm.
source: The precipitation is mainly concentrated between April and June with an average yearly rainfall of 1430 mm.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system's climate.

claim: The average annual temperature is 17 °C.
source: The average annual temperature is 17 °C (hottest from June to August) and the average daily temperature ranges from –7.6 °C in January to 41.8 °C in July (Si et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system's climate supported by a citation.

claim: 36 islands were selected according to a gradient of island area and isolation with no significant correlation between island area and isolation.
source: We selected 36 islands according to a gradient of island area and isolation with a guarantee of no significant correlation between island area and isolation (Pearson r=–0.21, p=0.21).
evidence: This describes the study design and sampling methodology.

claim: Distance to the mainland is the best distance-based measure in fitting species' colonization rate and extinction rate in TIL.
source: Distance to the mainland is the best distance-based measure in fitting species' colonization rate and extinction rate in TIL (Si et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research in the same system.

claim: Since lake formation, the islands have been protected by forbidding logging, allowing natural succession pathways to occur.
source: Since lake formation, the islands have been protected by forbidding logging, allowing natural succession pathways to occur.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system's management history.

claim: 53 survey transects were established on 36 islands with the sampling effort on each island roughly proportional to the logarithm of the island area.
source: We established 53 survey transects on 36 islands with the sampling effort on each island roughly proportional to the logarithm of the island area (Schoereder et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the study design and sampling methodology supported by a citation.

claim: Breeding bird communities were surveyed on each transect nine times annually (three times per month from April to June) from 2012 to 2021.
source: Breeding bird communities were surveyed on each transect nine times annually (three times per month from April to June) from 2012 to 2021 (Si et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology supported by a citation.

claim: Observers walked along each transect at a constant speed (2.0 km/hr) and recorded all the birds seen or heard on the survey islands.
source: In each survey, observers walked along each transect at a constant speed (2.0 km/hr) and recorded all the birds seen or heard on the survey islands.
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology.

claim: The abundance estimate was based on the maximum number of individuals recorded across the nine annual surveys.
source: We based our abundance estimate on the maximum number of individuals recorded across the nine annual surveys.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: Non-breeding species, nocturnal and crepuscular species, high-flying species passing over the islands, and strongly water-associated birds were excluded from the record.
source: We excluded non-breeding species, nocturnal and crepuscular species, high-flying species passing over the islands (e.g., raptors, swallows) and strongly water-associated birds (e.g., cormorants) from our record.
evidence: This describes the data filtering criteria.

claim: 60 species were finally retained after filtering.
source: Following these filtering, 60 species were finally retained.
evidence: This describes the final dataset after filtering.

claim: Climate data (monthly average temperature from 2012 to 2021) was obtained from the Meteorological Bureau of Chun'an County in Zhejiang Province, China.
source: We obtained climate data (monthly average temperature from 2012 to 2021) from the Meteorological Bureau of Chun'an County in Zhejiang Province, China.
evidence: This describes the source of climate data.

claim: Breeding season temperature was calculated as the average of the mean monthly temperature from April to June.
source: We calculated breeding season temperature as the average of the mean monthly temperature from April to June in order to represent the thermal conditions birds experience at this site each year (Lindström et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology supported by a citation.

claim: Breeding season temperature increased significantly over 10 years (slope = 0.078, r2=34.53%, p=0.04).
source: Breeding season temperature increased significantly over 10 years (slope = 0.078, r2=34.53%, p=0.04, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of climate data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: STI of a given species is defined as the average temperature of breeding months (April – June) across its distributional range (restricted to the Northern hemisphere) averaged over 1970–2000.
source: We followed the methods of Devictor et al., 2008 to calculate a species temperature index (STI) using ArcMap 10.3. STI of a given species is defined as the average temperature of breeding months (April – June) across its distributional range (restricted to the Northern hemisphere) averaged over 1970–2000.
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating STI supported by a citation.

claim: Monthly temperature data were obtained from WorldClim at a resolution of 30-arc seconds.
source: Monthly temperature data were obtained from WorldClim at a resolution of 30-arc seconds (http://www.worldclim.org).
evidence: This describes the source of temperature data for STI calculation.

claim: Distributional maps were extracted from Birdlife International 2019.
source: Distributional maps were extracted from Birdlife International 2019 (http://datazone.birdlife.org/species/requestdis), in which we selected only the distributional regions where the species is either resident or breeding.
evidence: This describes the source of distributional data for STI calculation.

claim: Species with STI higher than the median STI were labeled as warm-adapted species, and species lower than the median STI were labeled as cold-adapted species.
source: All species were divided into two groups indicating their relative thermal preference: species with STI higher than the median STI were labeled as warm-adapted species, and species lower than the median STI were labeled as cold-adapted species (Bates et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the classification methodology supported by a citation.

claim: The rank order of species STI is highly correlated across methods.
source: The STI of a species can differ depending on distributional and climate data but the rank order of species STI is highly correlated across methods (Barnagaud et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The robustness of STI calculations was verified using different distributional ranges and annual time windows.
source: We verified the robustness of our STI calculations using different distributional ranges and annual time windows (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a validation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CTI is a community-level index representing the average species thermal niche of all species or individuals in the community.
source: CTI is a community-level index representing the average species thermal niche of all species or individuals in the community (Devictor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: True abundance should be highly correlated with maximum observed abundance given high survey effort.
source: CTIoccur was calculated using occurrence data corrected for imperfect detection (see next section), while CTIabun was estimated using the maximum annual count across 9 surveys. Given that our survey effort was so high (i.e., 9 repeat surveys per year), true abundance should be highly correlated with maximum observed abundance (MacKenzie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by a citation.

claim: A spatially hierarchical dynamic multi-species occupancy model was developed in a Bayesian framework to account for imperfect detection.
source: Presence-absence data can be highly sensitive to false negatives, so to explore the driving processes of change in CTIoccur, and to explore how habitat fragmentation mediated the main processes while accounting for the imperfect detection, we developed a spatially hierarchical dynamic multi-species occupancy model (MSOM) in a Bayesian framework based on the model by Royle and Kéry, 2007.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology supported by a citation.

claim: Occupancy estimates are broadly interpreted as 'use' to relax the closure assumption.
source: However, given that individual birds move dynamically across territories within a year, during 9 surveys each year, we broadly interpret our estimates of 'occupancy' as 'use' (Si et al., 2018) to relax the closure assumption (MacKenzie et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a methodological clarification supported by citations.

claim: The Bayesian p-value was 0.488, indicating an unbiased estimation of the model.
source: We checked the posterior predictive ability of the model fit by calculating Bayesian p-values (p=0.488, indicating an unbiased estimation of our model; Gelman et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a result from model validation supported by a citation.

claim: Bayesian linear regression was used to derive a posterior estimate of the temporal trend in CTIoccur while propagating error in the estimation of CTIoccur.
source: To test for occurrence-based thermophilization at the island level, Bayesian linear regression using R2jags (Su and Yajima, 2021) was used to derive a posterior estimate of the temporal trend in CTIoccur while propagating error in the estimation of CTIoccur.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology supported by a citation.

claim: Linear mixed effect models with restricted maximum likelihood were used to model temporal trends in CTIabun.
source: To test for abundance-based thermophilization, linear mixed effect models (LMM) with restricted maximum likelihood (REML) were used to model temporal trends in CTIabun using function lme in R package nlme (Pinheiro et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology supported by a citation.

claim: The first-order correlation structure was included to account for temporal autocorrelation of CTI from the same island through time.
source: To account for the temporal autocorrelation of CTI from the same island through time, we included the first-order correlation structure (e.g. the corAR1 structure) because observations sampled from the nearby years may be more similar.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology to account for temporal autocorrelation.
